body.text:
The most expensive part of seborrheic keratoses isn't any single appointment. It's the moment you realize the appointments will never end and the count will never go down.

I stared at the total. $815, on seborrheic keratoses.

Then I did something I'd never done before. I opened the notes app on my phone and started adding up everything I'd spent on these spots over the past two years.

Six cryotherapy sessions. Two IPL consultations, one of which I went through with. A glycolic exfoliating stick that did nothing. A 20% urea foot cream someone on Reddit recommended. Two different AHA body lotions. A bottle of tea tree oil.

I stopped adding when the number hit $2,100.

Then I stood up, went into the bathroom, turned around, and tried to count the spots on my back in the mirror.

I couldn't get an accurate count because I couldn't see all of them. But from what I could see, plus the ones on my chest, my sides, my neck, my arms, I estimated somewhere around 80 to 90.

I sat back down with two numbers in front of me. $2,100 spent. Approximately 85 spots remaining.

Two years ago, when I started paying for removal, I had maybe 30.

I had spent $2,100 and had nearly three times as many spots as when I started spending.

I just sat there. Staring at the math. Because the math was telling me something I'd been feeling for months but hadn't let myself think through clearly.

This doesn't work. Not because the treatments are bad. Because the system is structurally broken.

My dermatologist freezes 6 to 8 spots per session at $250. In the 4 to 6 weeks between sessions, 5 to 10 new ones appear. Some of the frozen ones come back. And each session leaves pale marks where the spots used to be.

So every time I pay to move backward by 6, the problem moves forward by 8. And I trade brown raised spots for white flat marks. And the total count creeps higher anyway.

I grabbed a calculator. If I have 85 spots and she treats 7 per session at $250, that's 12 sessions just to address what's currently there. $3,000. Over the course of those 12 sessions, at the rate new ones appear, I'd accumulate roughly 40 to 60 more. So I'd finish the cycle with 40 to 60 untreated spots. Having spent $3,000.

Then I'd need another cycle. And another. And it would never end. Because the rate of arrival permanently exceeds the rate of removal.

I closed the calculator app. My hands were shaking a little. Not from fear. From the realization that I had been pouring money into something that was mathematically guaranteed to never catch up.

I'd been treating this like a solvable expense. Budget for a few sessions a year, keep the worst ones managed, stay ahead of it. But I wasn't staying ahead of it. The numbers proved I was falling behind and had been falling behind from the very first appointment.

The next morning I didn't call to book another session. For the first time in two years I stopped and asked a different question.

Why can't I manage all of them at once, at home, for a fraction of what one session costs?

That question led me to the research that changed how I understood the entire problem.

Seborrheic keratoses are compacted keratin. Dense, hardened protein structures bonded at a level that regular exfoliants and mild acids can't reach. A 7% glycolic stick is formulated for normal skin cell turnover. A 20% urea cream is a moisturizer. Neither one is concentrated enough to disrupt the bonds in compacted keratin. They work around the spots, not through them.

That's why every product I'd bought sat on the surface and did nothing to the actual structure of the growths. And that's why cryotherapy, which does destroy the growth, can't prevent new ones from forming. It addresses the output without changing the process.

The only way to manage all of them at home, at scale, affordably, is something concentrated enough to soften the compacted keratin structure itself. Not polish the surface. Not freeze one spot at a time. Soften the dense protein bonds across every spot, consistently, as part of a daily routine.

I found SK Renewal 40 through a forum thread where someone had done almost identical math to mine. Hundreds spent, count still climbing, system structurally broken. She'd switched to this and described it as the first time the economics of the problem actually made sense.

40% urea. At that concentration it crosses a functional threshold, stops being a moisturizer, becomes a keratolytic. It disrupts hydrogen bonds in compacted keratin, softening the dense structure from within. 2% salicylic acid loosens the keratinized cells once softened so they shed instead of sitting compressed.

Green tea extract and aloe calm and hydrate the skin after keratolytic action. Tea tree oil for the darkened tone. Coconut oil protects surrounding skin.

One jar. Every spot. Daily. For less than the copay of a single cryo session.

I ordered it and started applying it across everything. Back, chest, neck, sides, arms. A small amount on each spot, leave it on. All of them. At once.

By day seven a few of the flatter spots felt different under my fingers. Smoother at the edges. Less raised.

By week two I took photos and compared them to the ones from the month before. The difference was visible. Not dramatic. But the most prominent ones were lower, less defined, blending more into the surrounding skin.

By week three I ran my hand across my side where a cluster of five had always felt like a rough patch. For the first time, my hand passed over it without catching on raised edges.

Week four I opened my credit card statement. Zero dermatology charges. First time in two years.

I sat with that for a minute. Not because the money itself mattered that much. But because of what it represented. For two years, those charges had been proof that I was trying. But the math proved that trying wasn't the same as managing. I was buying the feeling of doing something while the problem outran every dollar I spent.

Now I was spending a fraction of one session on something that covered every spot simultaneously. And for the first time the trajectory was actually changing.

Two months in and I still open my credit card statement on Sunday nights. Old habit.

But now when I open it, the dermatology line is just, not there. It's been two months of not there. After two straight years of $250, $250, $315, $250.

I actually laughed the first time I noticed. Not a funny laugh. More like a, I can't believe I spent $2,100 on something that made the problem worse, kind of laugh.

Here's what gets me. I spent more on two cryo sessions than I've spent on this cream in two months. Two sessions that treated maybe 14 spots, left white marks, and watched half of them come back. Meanwhile the cream has been working on all 85 of them, every single night, and the total cost is less than my copay used to be.

The math finally makes sense. That's the part I keep coming back to. For two years the numbers never worked no matter how I calculated them. I'd add up sessions, count remaining spots, project forward, and every version of the math ended the same way. Falling behind.

Last week I did the count again. Not because I was anxious. Because I was curious.

It was lower than the time before. First time that's ever happened.

I closed the calculator app and just sat there smiling like an idiot. After two years of numbers going in the wrong direction, watching one finally go the other way felt like something I didn't know I was allowed to have.

EDIT: I keep getting the same DM over and over asking what the cream is called and where I bought it so I'm just going to put it here. I did not buy it on Amazon or Ebay, I got it directly from their website. Easier to just drop the link than keep copy pasting the same reply.

body.text:
The most expensive part of seborrheic keratoses isn't any single appointment. It's the moment you realize the appointments will never end and the count will never go down.

I stared at the total. $815, on seborrheic keratoses.

Then I did something I'd never done before. I opened the notes app on my phone and started adding up everything I'd spent on these spots over the past two years.

Six cryotherapy sessions. Two IPL consultations, one of which I went through with. A glycolic exfoliating stick that did nothing. A 20% urea foot cream someone on Reddit recommended. Two different AHA body lotions. A bottle of tea tree oil.

I stopped adding when the number hit $2,100.

Then I stood up, went into the bathroom, turned around, and tried to count the spots on my back in the mirror.

I couldn't get an accurate count because I couldn't see all of them. But from what I could see, plus the ones on my chest, my sides, my neck, my arms, I estimated somewhere around 80 to 90.

I sat back down with two numbers in front of me. $2,100 spent. Approximately 85 spots remaining.

Two years ago, when I started paying for removal, I had maybe 30.

I had spent $2,100 and had nearly three times as many spots as when I started spending.

I just sat there. Staring at the math. Because the math was telling me something I'd been feeling for months but hadn't let myself think through clearly.

This doesn't work. Not because the treatments are bad. Because the system is structurally broken.

My dermatologist freezes 6 to 8 spots per session at $250. In the 4 to 6 weeks between sessions, 5 to 10 new ones appear. Some of the frozen ones come back. And each session leaves pale marks where the spots used to be.

So every time I pay to move backward by 6, the problem moves forward by 8. And I trade brown raised spots for white flat marks. And the total count creeps higher anyway.

I grabbed a calculator. If I have 85 spots and she treats 7 per session at $250, that's 12 sessions just to address what's currently there. $3,000. Over the course of those 12 sessions, at the rate new ones appear, I'd accumulate roughly 40 to 60 more. So I'd finish the cycle with 40 to 60 untreated spots. Having spent $3,000.

Then I'd need another cycle. And another. And it would never end. Because the rate of arrival permanently exceeds the rate of removal.

I closed the calculator app. My hands were shaking a little. Not from fear. From the realization that I had been pouring money into something that was mathematically guaranteed to never catch up.

I'd been treating this like a solvable expense. Budget for a few sessions a year, keep the worst ones managed, stay ahead of it. But I wasn't staying ahead of it. The numbers proved I was falling behind and had been falling behind from the very first appointment.

The next morning I didn't call to book another session. For the first time in two years I stopped and asked a different question.

Why can't I manage all of them at once, at home, for a fraction of what one session costs?

That question led me to the research that changed how I understood the entire problem.

Seborrheic keratoses are compacted keratin. Dense, hardened protein structures bonded at a level that regular exfoliants and mild acids can't reach. A 7% glycolic stick is formulated for normal skin cell turnover. A 20% urea cream is a moisturizer. Neither one is concentrated enough to disrupt the bonds in compacted keratin. They work around the spots, not through them.

That's why every product I'd bought sat on the surface and did nothing to the actual structure of the growths. And that's why cryotherapy, which does destroy the growth, can't prevent new ones from forming. It addresses the output without changing the process.

The only way to manage all of them at home, at scale, affordably, is something concentrated enough to soften the compacted keratin structure itself. Not polish the surface. Not freeze one spot at a time. Soften the dense protein bonds across every spot, consistently, as part of a daily routine.

I found SK Renewal 40 through a forum thread where someone had done almost identical math to mine. Hundreds spent, count still climbing, system structurally broken. She'd switched to this and described it as the first time the economics of the problem actually made sense.

40% urea. At that concentration it crosses a functional threshold, stops being a moisturizer, becomes a keratolytic. It disrupts hydrogen bonds in compacted keratin, softening the dense structure from within. 2% salicylic acid loosens the keratinized cells once softened so they shed instead of sitting compressed.

Green tea extract and aloe calm and hydrate the skin after keratolytic action. Tea tree oil for the darkened tone. Coconut oil protects surrounding skin.

One jar. Every spot. Daily. For less than the copay of a single cryo session.

I ordered it and started applying it across everything. Back, chest, neck, sides, arms. A small amount on each spot, leave it on. All of them. At once.

By day seven a few of the flatter spots felt different under my fingers. Smoother at the edges. Less raised.

By week two I took photos and compared them to the ones from the month before. The difference was visible. Not dramatic. But the most prominent ones were lower, less defined, blending more into the surrounding skin.

By week three I ran my hand across my side where a cluster of five had always felt like a rough patch. For the first time, my hand passed over it without catching on raised edges.

Week four I opened my credit card statement. Zero dermatology charges. First time in two years.

I sat with that for a minute. Not because the money itself mattered that much. But because of what it represented. For two years, those charges had been proof that I was trying. But the math proved that trying wasn't the same as managing. I was buying the feeling of doing something while the problem outran every dollar I spent.

Now I was spending a fraction of one session on something that covered every spot simultaneously. And for the first time the trajectory was actually changing.

Two months in and I still open my credit card statement on Sunday nights. Old habit.

But now when I open it, the dermatology line is just, not there. It's been two months of not there. After two straight years of $250, $250, $315, $250.

I actually laughed the first time I noticed. Not a funny laugh. More like a, I can't believe I spent $2,100 on something that made the problem worse, kind of laugh.

Here's what gets me. I spent more on two cryo sessions than I've spent on this cream in two months. Two sessions that treated maybe 14 spots, left white marks, and watched half of them come back. Meanwhile the cream has been working on all 85 of them, every single night, and the total cost is less than my copay used to be.

The math finally makes sense. That's the part I keep coming back to. For two years the numbers never worked no matter how I calculated them. I'd add up sessions, count remaining spots, project forward, and every version of the math ended the same way. Falling behind.

Last week I did the count again. Not because I was anxious. Because I was curious.

It was lower than the time before. First time that's ever happened.

I closed the calculator app and just sat there smiling like an idiot. After two years of numbers going in the wrong direction, watching one finally go the other way felt like something I didn't know I was allowed to have.

body.text:
Last Tuesday at 1am I typed "how to get rid of seborrheic keratosis at home" into Google for what I'm fairly sure was the hundredth time.

I recognized the results before they loaded. Same dermatology websites. Same forum threads. Same product recommendations I'd already saved and never bought. I scrolled through them anyway, the way you scroll through a fridge you already know is empty.

I clicked on a Reddit thread I'd definitely read before. Read it again. Saved a comment I'd already saved. Closed the browser. Stared at the ceiling. Went to sleep.

Two nights later I did the exact same thing. Different search this time. "Best treatment for seborrheic keratoses 2024." Same results. Same threads. Same scroll. Same close. Same ceiling.

I didn't always do this.

Two years ago I wasn't searching. I was trying. Actually doing things. Actually spending money and booking appointments and buying products and believing each one might be the answer.

It started with cryotherapy. My dermatologist froze a group of them off for $250. She was thorough. Got maybe eight in one session. They healed. Left some pale marks. But the rough raised ones were gone and I thought I'd handled it.

A month later two of them came back. Same spots. And four new ones appeared in places that were clear before the appointment.

I went back. Another $250. Another round. Same result. They'd come back. New ones alongside them. White marks where the old ones had been.

So I tried other things. A glycolic exfoliating stick someone in a forum recommended. Used it every single day for six weeks. My skin felt smoother in general but the actual raised spots, the thick rough ones I was trying to flatten, didn't change at all. Not even slightly.

I tried an AHA body lotion. Two different brands actually, one after the other. Same story. General skin smoothness improved. The actual seborrheic keratoses, the compacted raised growths, completely unchanged.

I tried tea tree oil. Hydrogen peroxide. Apple cider vinegar on a cotton pad. One of those made the surrounding skin red and irritated while the spots sat there untouched, which felt like a cruel joke.

Each time something failed I felt a little less willing to try the next thing. And each time I felt a little more stupid for believing the last one would work.

That's when the searching started.

Not searching for a solution. Searching as a replacement for trying. Because trying meant spending money, waiting, hoping, and then standing in front of the mirror realizing nothing had changed. Searching felt safer. I could read about products without buying them. Save them without using them. Stay in the research phase forever and never risk another disappointment.

So that became my routine. Most weeks. Usually between 11pm and 1am. Usually after a shower where I noticed a new spot or felt one that seemed bigger. I'd get into bed, pick up my phone, and start the loop. Search, scroll, read, save, close. Sometimes I'd find a new thread. Sometimes a product I hadn't seen before. I'd screenshot it. Add it to a folder. Never order it.

I didn't realize how bad the pattern had gotten until last week, when I accidentally tapped my browser history instead of opening a new search.

I wish I hadn't looked.

The list went back months. And it was the same search, rephrased over and over, stretching down the screen.

"Seborrheic keratosis home removal."
"How to flatten seborrheic keratosis."
"Does glycolic acid work on SKs."
"Why won't my SKs go away."
"Seborrheic keratosis getting worse."
"SK treatment that actually works."

Dozens of entries. Sometimes the same exact search three days apart. Sometimes a slight variation, like rephrasing the question would somehow change the answer.

I sat there and recognized what I was looking at. It was the search history of someone who had tried everything the forums recommended, watched all of it fail, and then replaced trying with searching because searching couldn't disappoint her.

I had over 60 spots across my back, chest, and sides. Three years ago I had maybe 15. I'd spent hundreds on cryo, hundreds on products, months of nightly research. And I had four times as many spots as when I started.

That night, staring at my own browser history, I decided to change the question. Not "what product should I try next." I'd been asking that for a year and the answers had all failed. Instead I typed something I'd never typed before.

"Why don't creams work on seborrheic keratoses."

The answer was in a forum post from a woman who described the same loop I'd been in. Same failed products too. Glycolic stick, check. Urea foot cream, check. AHA lotion, check. Cryotherapy, check. Year of nightly searching, check.

She said she'd been circling the same way until she understood one thing. Seborrheic keratoses are not rough skin. They're compacted keratin. Dense, hardened protein structures bonded at a level that regular exfoliants and mild acids physically cannot reach.

She explained that glycolic sticks at low concentrations are formulated for normal skin cell turnover. They smooth the surface layer. But the compacted keratin that forms an SK sits underneath that surface, densely bonded, structurally resistant to anything that isn't concentrated enough to disrupt it. You can apply a mild acid every day for a year and the dense structure underneath won't change because the product is working on the wrong layer at the wrong strength.

That's why the glycolic stick failed. That's why the AHA lotions failed. That's why the drugstore urea cream failed, at low concentrations urea just moisturizes. It doesn't break keratin bonds.

And cryotherapy destroys the visible growth but doesn't change the skin's keratin production. Which is why they came back every single time.

I read that paragraph and felt something shift. Not excitement. Clarity. For the first time I wasn't reading about a product. I was reading about why every product I'd tried, and every product I'd saved and never bought, would have failed for the same structural reason.

Wrong concentration. Wrong layer. Wrong mechanism entirely.

She said there's a threshold where urea stops moisturizing and starts actually breaking down compacted keratin. It disrupts hydrogen bonds in the dense protein structure, softening it from within instead of polishing above it. Combined with salicylic acid that loosens the keratinized cells once softened so they shed instead of sitting compressed.

The product she named was SK Renewal 40. She said it also had green tea and aloe for calming the skin after keratolytic action, tea tree oil for evening out darkened tone, and coconut oil for protecting surrounding skin.

She said the reason she finally ordered it after her own year of circling was that the mechanism explanation collapsed every question she'd been asking into one answer. Everything she'd tried had been too weak to reach the structural level where the problem actually exists. Once she understood that, the loop broke. There was nothing left to search for.

I read her post sitting in bed at 11:47pm. The same bed where I'd done hundreds of pointless searches. The same phone. The same time of night.

But for the first time I didn't close the browser and stare at the ceiling. I ordered it.

The first week I refused to check obsessively for results. I'd spent enough time checking. I was tired of watching for miracles that didn't come.

Around day eight I was in the shower and ran my fingers across the cluster on my left side. The edges were softer. Less defined. The rough texture that used to catch under my fingertips felt different.

By week two I could see it. The flatter spots on my chest were less raised, less contrasted against the surrounding skin. I took a photo because after everything that had failed, I needed proof I wasn't imagining it.

I wasn't imagining it.

By week three the raised spots on my back had softened enough that when I reached behind my shoulder I couldn't immediately locate them by touch. I had to actually feel around for them. That had never happened before. Not after the glycolic stick. Not after the AHA lotion. Not after the urea foot cream. Not after any of it.

Week four I was lying in bed at 11pm. Same time. Same phone. I opened my browser out of pure habit. My thumb went to the search bar automatically.

And I just sat there. Smiling like an idiot at my own phone. Because for the first time in over a year I had absolutely nothing to type.

Not because I gave up. Because every single question I'd been asking, every rephrased search, every 1am scroll session, every screenshot I saved and never acted on, all of it was the same question asked a hundred different ways. And it finally got answered.

I checked my browser history the next morning just to see it. My last skin-related search was five weeks ago. Before that it was every two to three days. A year of nightly spiraling and then just, silence. I keep looking at that gap the way you look at a bank account after you finally stop bleeding money. It's the most satisfying nothing I've ever seen.

Here's the part that makes me emotional when I think about it. I almost didn't order it. After everything that failed, after the glycolic stick and the AHA lotion and the foot cream and the cryotherapy and the hundreds of dollars, I almost added SK Renewal 40 to the screenshot folder and kept scrolling. Almost did the same thing I'd done every night for a year. Save it. Close the browser. Stare at the ceiling.

I'm so glad I didn't.

I spent a year searching for something that worked. Turns out the hardest part wasn't finding it. It was believing it existed long enough to actually try it.

The most expensive part of seborrheic keratoses isn't any single appointment. It's the moment you realize the appointments will never end and the count will never go down.

I stared at the total. $815, on seborrheic keratoses.

Then I did something I'd never done before. I opened the notes app on my phone and started adding up everything I'd spent on these spots over the past two years.

Six cryotherapy sessions. Two IPL consultations, one of which I went through with. A glycolic exfoliating stick that did nothing. A 20% urea foot cream someone on Reddit recommended. Two different AHA body lotions. A bottle of tea tree oil.

I stopped adding when the number hit $2,100.

Then I stood up, went into the bathroom, turned around, and tried to count the spots on my back in the mirror.

I couldn't get an accurate count because I couldn't see all of them. But from what I could see, plus the ones on my chest, my sides, my neck, my arms, I estimated somewhere around 80 to 90.

I sat back down with two numbers in front of me. $2,100 spent. Approximately 85 spots remaining.

Two years ago, when I started paying for removal, I had maybe 30.

I had spent $2,100 and had nearly three times as many spots as when I started spending.

I just sat there. Staring at the math. Because the math was telling me something I'd been feeling for months but hadn't let myself think through clearly.

This doesn't work. Not because the treatments are bad. Because the system is structurally broken.

My dermatologist freezes 6 to 8 spots per session at $250. In the 4 to 6 weeks between sessions, 5 to 10 new ones appear. Some of the frozen ones come back. And each session leaves pale marks where the spots used to be.

So every time I pay to move backward by 6, the problem moves forward by 8. And I trade brown raised spots for white flat marks. And the total count creeps higher anyway.

I grabbed a calculator. If I have 85 spots and she treats 7 per session at $250, that's 12 sessions just to address what's currently there. $3,000. Over the course of those 12 sessions, at the rate new ones appear, I'd accumulate roughly 40 to 60 more. So I'd finish the cycle with 40 to 60 untreated spots. Having spent $3,000.

Then I'd need another cycle. And another. And it would never end. Because the rate of arrival permanently exceeds the rate of removal.

I closed the calculator app. My hands were shaking a little. Not from fear. From the realization that I had been pouring money into something that was mathematically guaranteed to never catch up.

I'd been treating this like a solvable expense. Budget for a few sessions a year, keep the worst ones managed, stay ahead of it. But I wasn't staying ahead of it. The numbers proved I was falling behind and had been falling behind from the very first appointment.

The next morning I didn't call to book another session. For the first time in two years I stopped and asked a different question.

Why can't I manage all of them at once, at home, for a fraction of what one session costs?

That question led me to the research that changed how I understood the entire problem.

Seborrheic keratoses are compacted keratin. Dense, hardened protein structures bonded at a level that regular exfoliants and mild acids can't reach. A 7% glycolic stick is formulated for normal skin cell turnover. A 20% urea cream is a moisturizer. Neither one is concentrated enough to disrupt the bonds in compacted keratin. They work around the spots, not through them.

That's why every product I'd bought sat on the surface and did nothing to the actual structure of the growths. And that's why cryotherapy, which does destroy the growth, can't prevent new ones from forming. It addresses the output without changing the process.

The only way to manage all of them at home, at scale, affordably, is something concentrated enough to soften the compacted keratin structure itself. Not polish the surface. Not freeze one spot at a time. Soften the dense protein bonds across every spot, consistently, as part of a daily routine.

I found SK Renewal 40 through a forum thread where someone had done almost identical math to mine. Hundreds spent, count still climbing, system structurally broken. She'd switched to this and described it as the first time the economics of the problem actually made sense.

40% urea. At that concentration it crosses a functional threshold, stops being a moisturizer, becomes a keratolytic. It disrupts hydrogen bonds in compacted keratin, softening the dense structure from within. 2% salicylic acid loosens the keratinized cells once softened so they shed instead of sitting compressed.

Green tea extract and aloe calm and hydrate the skin after keratolytic action. Tea tree oil for the darkened tone. Coconut oil protects surrounding skin.

One jar. Every spot. Daily. For less than the copay of a single cryo session.

I ordered it and started applying it across everything. Back, chest, neck, sides, arms. A small amount on each spot, leave it on. All of them. At once.

By day seven a few of the flatter spots felt different under my fingers. Smoother at the edges. Less raised.

By week two I took photos and compared them to the ones from the month before. The difference was visible. Not dramatic. But the most prominent ones were lower, less defined, blending more into the surrounding skin.

By week three I ran my hand across my side where a cluster of five had always felt like a rough patch. For the first time, my hand passed over it without catching on raised edges.

Week four I opened my credit card statement. Zero dermatology charges. First time in two years.

I sat with that for a minute. Not because the money itself mattered that much. But because of what it represented. For two years, those charges had been proof that I was trying. But the math proved that trying wasn't the same as managing. I was buying the feeling of doing something while the problem outran every dollar I spent.

Now I was spending a fraction of one session on something that covered every spot simultaneously. And for the first time the trajectory was actually changing.

Two months in and I still open my credit card statement on Sunday nights. Old habit.

But now when I open it, the dermatology line is just, not there. It's been two months of not there. After two straight years of $250, $250, $315, $250.

I actually laughed the first time I noticed. Not a funny laugh. More like a, I can't believe I spent $2,100 on something that made the problem worse, kind of laugh.

Here's what gets me. I spent more on two cryo sessions than I've spent on this cream in two months. Two sessions that treated maybe 14 spots, left white marks, and watched half of them come back. Meanwhile the cream has been working on all 85 of them, every single night, and the total cost is less than my copay used to be.

The math finally makes sense. That's the part I keep coming back to. For two years the numbers never worked no matter how I calculated them. I'd add up sessions, count remaining spots, project forward, and every version of the math ended the same way. Falling behind.

Last week I did the count again. Not because I was anxious. Because I was curious.

It was lower than the time before. First time that's ever happened.

I closed the calculator app and just sat there smiling like an idiot. After two years of numbers going in the wrong direction, watching one finally go the other way felt like something I didn't know I was allowed to have.
